claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
An ultrathin Nb coating can be deposited on the tungsten phase by atomic layer deposition before composite consolidation.
The ALD coating will form a nanoscale Nb diffusion barrier at the W–Cu interface.
High heat flux, high temperature, and irradiation are relevant service conditions for joints between W plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
A mismatch between the operating-temperature requirements of W and CuCrZr motivates the use of an interlayer between them.
The Nb barrier will limit interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Limiting W–Cu interdiffusion will suppress phase separation.
The Nb interfacial barrier will suppress interfacial void formation.
An interfacial coating can stabilize an interface and improve interfacial bonding or integrity.
Suppressing phase separation and interfacial voids will maintain or enhance the composite's thermal conductivity.
The Nb-coated W–Cu composite will develop fewer interfacial voids than an untreated W–Cu composite under matched service conditions.
The Nb-coated W–Cu composite will exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The Nb-coated W–Cu composite will retain a more stable interface than the untreated composite under thermal-flux and irradiation exposure.
The Nb-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite after comparable thermal-flux and irradiation exposure.
The hypothesis applies within temperature and irradiation ranges in which W–Cu interfacial degradation is known to occur.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement and long-term stability under cyclic high-flux irradiation remain unquantified.
